You are a senior analyst using Claude to analyze requirements from several stakeholder sources.

Which is the correct order of steps?
(1) Group related requirements and flag conflicts or ambiguities for stakeholder review.
(2) Validate the structured output against the original sources for accuracy and completeness.
(3) Submit the consolidated inputs to Claude with a structured extraction prompt.
(4) Gather and label the source materials so each requirement can be traced.
(5) Document the final requirements set with source traceability and status.

Options.reason: Incorrect. Requirements can't be grouped and flagged (1) before they've even been extracted from Claude (3).
Correct. Gather/label sources, submit to Claude for structured extraction, group/flag conflicts, validate against originals, then document the final set.
Incorrect. You can't group requirements (1) before they've been gathered/labeled (4) or extracted (3) in the first place.
Incorrect. Source materials must be gathered and labeled (4) before you can submit them to Claude (3) for extraction.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: Requirements analysis flows: gather and label sources (4) -> extract via Claude (3) -> group and flag conflicts (1) -> validate against originals (2) -> document the final traceable set (5).

questions.Question:
You are a marketing manager deciding what to include in custom instructions for a writing-focused Project.

Which two items belong in the custom instructions? (Select 2)

Options.text: A representative sample of past writing that reflects the team's preferred style and structure.
Options.reason: Incorrect. While style samples can be helpful reference material, the two best-fit answers here are the brand voice/tone and structure/length expectations directly.

Options.text: The brand voice and tonal expectations the writing must follow.
Options.reason: Correct. Brand voice and tone are foundational, stable expectations that belong in Project-level custom instructions.

Options.text: The preferred writing style of the marketing manager who will review all final deliverables.
Options.reason: Incorrect. One individual reviewer's personal preference is not the same as the organization's established brand/style requirements.

Options.text: The prompt author's preferred response length for internal messages unrelated to external deliverables.
Options.reason: Incorrect. This is unrelated to the actual deliverables the writing-focused Project exists to support.

Options.text: The standard structure and length expectations for typical deliverables.
Options.reason: Correct. Standard structure and length expectations ensure consistent, on-brand formatting across every writing task in the Project.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: Project-level custom instructions should capture stable, organization-wide expectations -- brand voice/tone and standard structure/length -- rather than one individual's personal preferences or unrelated internal-message conventions.

questions.Question:
An HR business partner is configuring a new Project for recurring policy questions from managers. The Project will be used across many chats by several HR team members.

Which content belongs in the Project knowledge base?

Options.text: The current employee handbook plus prior versions of the handbook going back five years, so Claude can answer questions about how policies have changed.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Including outdated handbooks risks Claude citing obsolete rules and creating contradictions.

Options.text: The current employee handbook, the leveling guide, the policies-FAQ, and every email the HR team has sent about policy in the past year, for additional context.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Raw email trails inject uncurated noise, conflicting statements, and potential privacy issues into the knowledge base.

Options.text: The current employee handbook only, with the leveling guide and the policies-FAQ attached at the start of each chat as needed for that chat's topic.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Relegating core, frequently used documents to manual per-chat uploads undermines the efficiency benefit of using a Project.

Options.text: The current employee handbook, the leveling guide, and the policies-FAQ document referenced across the Project's chats.
Options.reason: Correct. These are the core, evergreen, authoritative reference documents that should live in the persistent knowledge base.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: The Project knowledge base should hold authoritative, canonical, frequently-accessed reference material -- the current handbook, leveling guide, and FAQ -- not outdated versions, raw email trails, or documents relegated to manual per-chat uploads.

questions.Question:
A learning specialist is configuring a Project for course-design work. Their organization has an internal instructional-design standard and a preferred output structure for lesson outlines.

Which custom-instruction set best supports this use case?

Options.text: Name Claude's role as a course designer; let each chat's prompt specify the standards and output structure for that lesson, since lessons vary widely.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Leaving standards and structure to individual chat prompts risks inconsistent results across the team.

Options.text: Name Claude's role as a course designer and require alignment to the organization's instructional-design standards; leave output structure to Claude based on the topic of each lesson.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Leaving structure fully to Claude's discretion can produce outlines that don't match the organization's required format.

Options.text: Specify only the preferred output structure for lesson outlines, since the structure carries the standards implicitly and naming the role adds no value.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Structure alone doesn't convey the full instructional-design standard, and role framing does add useful context.

Options.text: Name Claude's role as a course designer, require alignment to the organization's instructional-design standards, and specify the preferred output structure for lesson outlines.
Options.reason: Correct. Together, role, standards, and structure establish consistent expertise, quality criteria, and formatting across every course-design conversation.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: Comprehensive custom instructions combining role, standards, and structure produce consistent results across the Project -- putting any one piece only in individual prompts, or leaving structure to chance, risks inconsistency.

questions.Question:
You are a knowledge worker transitioning from a long, drifting conversation into a fresh focused session.

Which is the correct order of transition steps?
(1) Begin a new chat and paste the summary as its starting context.
(2) Summarize the goals, key decisions, and open questions from the long conversation.
(3) Identify which references should persist beyond the current chat.
(4) Move persistent references into a Project's knowledge base or attach them as needed.
(5) Confirm the new chat is on-task before continuing the work.

Options.reason: Incorrect. You need to summarize (2) and identify persistent references (3) before starting the new chat (1), not after.
Correct. Summarize the old conversation, identify what should persist, move it into the Project/attachments, start the new chat with the summary, then confirm on-task.
Incorrect. You need to identify which references should persist (3) before you can move them (4), not after.
Incorrect. Summarizing goals/decisions/questions (2) should generally come before identifying persistent references (3), since the summary often reveals what matters most.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: The transition flow: summarize the prior conversation (2) -> identify what should persist (3) -> move it into a Project/attach as needed (4) -> start the new chat with that summary (1) -> confirm the new session is on-task (5).

questions.Question:
A manager is deciding what changes to make while conducting a memory maintenance review for a long-running workflow.

Which two actions best support memory quality over time? (Choose 2)

Options.text: Delete all memories as the maintenance action to ensure a clean slate, then allow Claude to rebuild context organically through subsequent workflow runs.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Wiping everything discards useful, still-relevant context along with the stale entries.

Options.text: Disable Memory entirely to eliminate the risk of stale entries surfacing in future workflow runs.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Disabling Memory entirely sacrifices its benefits rather than maintaining its quality.

Options.text: Identify and edit or delete entries that are stale, inaccurate, or no longer relevant, and add context Claude has not automatically captured but the workflow continues to need.
Options.reason: Correct. Targeted curation -- removing what's stale and adding what's missing -- is the actual maintenance action that improves memory quality.

Options.text: Leave all memories untouched on the basis that the workflow has been running consistently and no output quality issues have been reported.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Absence of reported issues doesn't mean stale or inaccurate entries aren't quietly degrading quality.

Options.text: Export the current memories as a backup before making changes, so prior context can be restored if a maintenance edit unintentionally removes information the workflow still depends on.
Options.reason: Correct. Backing up before editing protects against accidentally losing information the workflow still needs.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: Good memory maintenance means targeted curation (removing stale/inaccurate entries, adding missing context) combined with backing up beforehand -- not wholesale deletion, disabling Memory, or leaving it untouched indefinitely.

questions.topic: Feature Choice for Persistent Team Reference
questions.Question:
An HR business partner is building a long-running workspace where a team handbook, a leveling guide, and a policies-FAQ document will be referenced across many separate chats by several team members.

Which Claude feature is designed for this use case?

Options.text: Connect the team's Google Drive folder where the three documents live, so the connector surfaces them inside each chat at the moment the chat needs them.
Options.reason: Incorrect. A connector surfaces documents dynamically but isn't the purpose-built feature for a shared, persistent team workspace with its own instructions.

Options.text: Generate an Artifact containing the three documents, which gives the team an editable surface for the reference content that persists across chats.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Artifacts are for specific generated content within a chat, not a shared, cross-team persistent knowledge workspace.

Options.text: Create a Project, which provides a persistent workspace with its own knowledge base and custom instructions shared across chats and members.
Options.reason: Correct. A Project is exactly the feature designed for a persistent, shared workspace with its own knowledge base and instructions across many chats and team members.

Options.text: Attach all three documents to each chat as needed, since per-chat attachments give the chat direct access to the documents without additional setup.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Per-chat attachments require repetitive manual setup and don't provide the persistent, shared workspace the use case calls for.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: A Project is purpose-built for exactly this scenario: a persistent workspace with its own knowledge base and custom instructions, shared consistently across many chats and multiple team members.

questions.topic: First Maintenance Action for Project Drift
questions.Question:
You are an operations lead and notice that a Project's outputs have been drifting from the team's current expectations.

Which maintenance action should be tried first?

Options.text: Review the Project's instructions and reference materials against current standards.
Options.reason: Correct. Checking whether the Project's instructions/knowledge base have fallen out of sync with current standards is the natural first diagnostic step.

Options.text: Switch the Project to a different Claude model in the hope it behaves better.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Switching models without diagnosing the actual cause is a guess, not a maintenance action.

Options.text: Continue using the Project and accept the drift as the new baseline of behavior.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Accepting drift without investigation lets a real configuration problem persist.

Options.text: Retire the Project and rebuild a new one from scratch with fresh content.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Rebuilding from scratch is a drastic, wasteful step before you've even diagnosed what's actually out of date.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: When outputs drift from expectations, the first, most targeted maintenance action is reviewing the Project's instructions and reference materials against current standards -- not switching models, ignoring it, or rebuilding entirely.

questions.Question:
You are writing system-level instructions for a Project that supports recurring writing tasks.

Which step should be performed first when writing the system-level instructions?

Options.text: Refine the drafted instructions based on observed gaps from validation runs.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Refinement depends on validation results existing first, which in turn depends on a draft existing.

Options.text: Validate the drafted instructions against representative requests for the Project.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Validation requires a draft of the instructions to already exist, and a clear purpose/boundary to validate against.

Options.text: Distribute the finalized instructions to collaborators on the Project.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Distribution is the last step, after drafting, validating, and refining.

Options.text: Define the purpose of the Project and the boundaries the instructions must respect.
Options.reason: Correct. Establishing the Project's purpose and boundaries first gives you the foundation for everything that follows -- drafting, testing, and refining.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: Defining the Project's purpose and boundaries must come first -- it establishes what the instructions need to accomplish before you draft, validate, refine, or distribute them.

questions.topic: First Step Configuring a New Project
questions.Question:
You are configuring a new Claude Project for a specific recurring workload.

Which Project configuration step should be performed first?

Options.text: Add reference materials and instructions that the Project will rely on.
Options.reason: Incorrect. You need to know the Project's purpose and workload first to know which materials/instructions are actually relevant.

Options.text: Invite collaborators to the Project and confirm the appropriate access levels.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Inviting collaborators before the Project's requirements are established can create unnecessary access or rework later.

Options.text: Test the configured Project on a representative request from the workload.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Testing requires the Project to already be configured, which requires the purpose and requirements to be defined first.

Options.text: Define the purpose of the Project and the recurring tasks it must support.
Options.reason: Correct. Establishing purpose and scope first provides the foundation for selecting instructions, materials, collaborators, and validation requests.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: As with system-level instructions, Project configuration starts with defining purpose and recurring workload -- everything else (materials, collaborators, testing) follows from that foundation.

questions.Question:
A knowledge worker often switches between Claude and another AI service while working on a long-running project.

Which Claude feature most directly reduces repetitive context-setting between sessions?

Options.text: Rely on a single static Artifact pasted into each chat as the only continuity mechanism, ignoring the Memory feature that is purpose-built for retaining work-relevant context across sessions.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Repeatedly pasting a static Artifact into every session doesn't provide the automatic continuity Memory is built for.

Options.text: Disable Memory entirely and re-paste the same context paragraphs at the start of every Claude session, even though Memory is designed to retain that context across conversations automatically.
Options.reason: Incorrect. This manually recreates the exact repetitive work Memory is designed to eliminate.

Options.text: Open every Claude session in Incognito mode, which prevents the conversation from contributing to Memory and therefore eliminates the cross-session continuity the project would benefit from.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Incognito mode actively works against cross-session continuity, the opposite of what's needed here.

Options.text: Enable Memory and use the import capability to bring relevant context from the other AI service into Claude as a starting point for the project's work.
Options.reason: Correct. Enabling Memory and importing context from the other service directly reduces the need to repeatedly re-establish context.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: Memory is purpose-built to retain relevant context across sessions, and its import capability lets you bring in context from another AI service as a starting point -- directly reducing repetitive context-setting.

questions.Question:
You are organizing connected data sources for a team and must complete the planning steps before authorizing any connection.

Which two planning steps must be completed BEFORE authorizing a new Connector? (Select 2)

Options.text: Decommission any unused legacy Connectors that may still be authorized.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Decommissioning old connectors is good hygiene, but it's not a prerequisite for authorizing a new one.

Options.text: Migrate every existing report off the prior data source onto the new Connector.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Migration is an implementation activity that happens after authorization, not before.

Options.text: Confirm the data classification of the source and the team's permission to use it.
Options.reason: Correct. Understanding data sensitivity and confirming the team has the right to access it is essential before granting any connection.

Options.text: Confirm the Connector is on the approved-vendor list maintained by IT.
Options.reason: Correct. Verifying vendor approval ensures the connection complies with organizational security and vendor-management requirements.

Options.text: Train every team member on the new Connector through formal training sessions.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Formal training may be useful eventually, but it isn't a prerequisite for authorizing the connection itself.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: Before authorizing a new Connector, you must confirm both the data classification/permission (is this data appropriate to connect?) and that the vendor is IT-approved -- migration, decommissioning, and training all happen at other points in the process.

questions.Question:
A knowledge worker is explaining the cost, speed, and quality trade-offs across Claude models to a colleague.

Which generalization correctly describes the trade-off?

Options.text: More capable models generally consume more resources and run more slowly, while lighter models are usually faster and less expensive.
Options.reason: Correct. This is the standard, accurate trade-off: greater capability generally costs more in latency and resource/rate-limit consumption.

Options.text: More capable models generally consume less of the usage limit because their reasoning is more efficient, even though they run more slowly than lighter models.
Options.reason: Incorrect. More capable models generally consume more of the usage limit, not less -- this inverts the actual relationship.

Options.text: Lighter models consume more resources per request than more capable models because they always require multiple passes to match higher-model quality.
Options.reason: Incorrect. This misrepresents how lighter models work -- they don't inherently require multiple passes, and they consume fewer resources per request.

Options.text: Speed and resource consumption are independent of model capability; the difference between Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus is reasoning depth alone.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Speed and resource consumption are directly tied to model capability, not independent of it.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: The standard trade-off holds: more capable models (like Opus) generally consume more resources and run more slowly, while lighter models (like Haiku) are faster and cheaper -- though at the cost of some reasoning depth.

questions.topic: Preserving Context Window with Regulatory Documents
questions.Question:
You are a research associate preparing inputs for a long task that references two lengthy regulatory documents, but only specific sections apply.

Which approach best preserves context-window capacity?

Options.text: Skip the documents entirely and rely on Claude to invent the missing context.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Skipping real source documents entirely and having Claude invent context risks fabricated, inaccurate information.

Options.text: Split each document into one-character pieces and feed them one at a time.
Options.reason: Incorrect. This is an absurd, impractical approach that would waste enormous context capacity.

Options.text: Extract only the relevant sections from each document and include those, omitting unrelated chapters.
Options.reason: Correct. Extracting only the applicable sections keeps the context focused and preserves capacity for other useful content.

Options.text: Paste the full text of both documents without trimming to maximize available material.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Pasting full, largely irrelevant text wastes context-window capacity that could be used more effectively.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: When only specific sections of lengthy documents actually apply, extracting just those relevant sections preserves context-window capacity far better than pasting entire documents or omitting them altogether.

questions.Question:
A finance manager must select a Claude feature for a task that requires deterministic calculations across a multi-tab spreadsheet.

Which selection best fits the requirement?

Options.text: Use an Artifact alone for the calculations, which provides a stable editable surface for the result but does not perform the deterministic computation that Code Execution would run.
Options.reason: Incorrect. An Artifact is a display/editing surface, not a computation engine.

Options.text: Use Code Execution, which runs code in a sandbox to perform calculations on the uploaded file and produce verified outputs the associate can check.
Options.reason: Correct. Code Execution runs actual code against the data, producing deterministic, verifiable calculations -- exactly what's required.

Options.text: Use the Research feature for the calculations, which gathers and synthesizes external sources and is not the appropriate feature for deterministic computation on an uploaded spreadsheet.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Research is designed for gathering/synthesizing external information, not running deterministic calculations on an uploaded file.

Options.text: Use a standard chat prompt for the calculations, which generates text without running code and does not produce the verified deterministic output the multi-tab calculation task requires.
Options.reason: Incorrect. A standard text-generation prompt cannot guarantee the precision and verifiability that deterministic calculations require.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: Deterministic, verifiable calculations on structured data require Code Execution, which actually runs code in a sandbox against the file -- not a standard chat prompt, an Artifact alone, or the Research feature.

questions.Question:
An analyst has been asked to compute summary statistics from an uploaded sales data file and produce a chart for a weekly report.

Which output approach best fits the task?

Options.text: Use Code Execution to perform the calculations and generate the chart, then verify the computed results against the source data before sharing the output.
Options.reason: Correct. Code Execution processes the full dataset, computes accurate statistics, and generates an actual chart -- with verification as a final check.

Options.text: Request a narrative description of the data in the chat response without computing values, leaving the summary statistics and the chart unproduced and the weekly report incomplete.
Options.reason: Incorrect. A narrative description doesn't fulfill the explicit requirement for computed statistics and an actual chart.

Options.text: Ask Claude to estimate the summary statistics from a brief preview of the file, accepting unverified figures rather than running the calculations against the full uploaded dataset.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Estimating from a preview risks inaccurate results, especially with many records; calculations should run against the full dataset.

Options.text: Produce a written placeholder for the chart in the chat response without generating the actual visualization, leaving the weekly report without the visual output it requires.
Options.reason: Incorrect. A placeholder doesn't satisfy the actual requirement to produce a real chart.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: Code Execution is the right approach when accurate calculations and real visualizations are needed -- it processes the full dataset, computes verified statistics, and generates the actual chart, unlike estimation, narrative description, or placeholders.

questions.Question:
You are an operations lead mapping production tasks to Claude model strengths to set realistic expectations.

Which two production tasks fit Claude's strengths most clearly? (Select 2)

Options.text: Synthesizing a single executive summary across many long source documents.
Options.reason: Correct. Large-context comprehension and synthesis across many documents is a core Claude strength.

Options.text: Monitoring a live sensor data stream and flagging anomalies as they occur in real time.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Real-time continuous stream monitoring requires specialized stream-processing infrastructure, not Claude's core strength.

Options.text: Drafting a tone-and-audience-aware customer-facing email under human review.
Options.reason: Correct. Adapting written communication for tone and audience, with human review as a safeguard, plays directly to Claude's strengths.

Options.text: Issuing a binding legal determination based solely on Claude's analysis of case documents.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Binding legal determinations require qualified human professionals and legal authority Claude cannot provide.

Options.text: Calculating the precise settlement value of a derivative contract using live market inputs.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Precise financial calculations with live market data require specialized, validated financial systems, not a general-purpose model.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: Claude's clearest production strengths are synthesizing large volumes of source material and drafting tone/audience-aware content under human review -- not autonomous real-time monitoring, binding legal determinations, or precise live financial calculations.

questions.topic: Model Selection for Recurring Meeting Summaries
questions.Question:
You are an operations assistant selecting a model for a recurring meeting-summary task that does not require deep reasoning and runs at moderate volume.

Which selection best balances cost, speed, and quality?

Options.text: Haiku, which is suitable only when the task requires the fastest possible turnaround.
Options.reason: Incorrect. This overstates Haiku's narrow fit and undersells Sonnet's suitability for everyday, moderate-volume work.

Options.text: Opus, which prioritizes depth at higher latency and rate-limit consumption.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Opus's extra depth isn't needed here and comes at unnecessary cost and latency for a task that doesn't require deep reasoning.

Options.text: Sonnet, which provides solid quality at moderate latency and rate-limit consumption for everyday work.
Options.reason: Correct. Sonnet is designed as the balanced, everyday-work option -- ideal for moderate-volume tasks that don't need deep reasoning.

Options.text: A custom model, which the Associate-level user would need to build and train independently.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Building a custom model is unnecessary and impractical for a straightforward summarization task.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: For a recurring, moderate-volume task not requiring deep reasoning, Sonnet's balance of solid quality, moderate latency, and moderate rate-limit consumption is the best fit -- Opus is overkill and Haiku is better suited to the fastest, lightest tasks.

questions.topic: Compliance Configuration for Sensitive Chatbot Data
questions.Question:
Your organization is evaluating Claude for a customer service chatbot that handles sensitive personal information (account details, transaction history). Your compliance team requires that no sensitive data should remain in conversation history after 90 days, and you need audit trails for all data access.

Which combination of configuration and governance measures best addresses these requirements?

Options.text: Configure Claude with system-level instructions to not retain data, then implement a separate data retention policy and audit logging system in your application layer.
Options.reason: Correct. Data retention and audit logging are infrastructure-level responsibilities that must be implemented in your own application systems alongside Claude's configuration.

Options.text: Trust Claude's built-in automatic deletion to handle all compliance requirements without additional system configuration.
Options.reason: Incorrect. This incorrectly assumes Claude manages compliance automatically; compliance responsibility ultimately lies with the deploying organization.

Options.text: Remove all sensitive data from prompts and rely only on Claude's training data for responses.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Legitimate customer service often requires working with sensitive data; avoidance isn't a practical governance strategy.

Options.text: Store all conversation history indefinitely in a database and let Claude handle compliance through API calls.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Indefinite storage with no explicit policy leaves the system vulnerable to data sprawl with no audit trail.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: Compliance requires a layered approach: system-level instructions can guide Claude's handling of data in the moment, but retention windows and audit logging are infrastructure-level obligations the deploying organization must implement itself.

questions.topic: Data Handling Sequence for Mixed-Sensitivity Document
questions.Question:
You are handling a document containing mixed-sensitivity content before using it with Claude.

Which data-handling step should be performed first?

Options.text: Redact sensitive fields and replace them with appropriate placeholders.
Options.reason: Incorrect. You can't redact fields accurately until you've first classified which fields are actually sensitive.

Options.text: Classify the content of the document and identify which fields are sensitive.
Options.reason: Correct. Classification -- identifying what's actually sensitive (PII, PHI, confidential data) -- must happen before any redaction can be done properly.

Options.text: Submit the redacted document to Claude for the intended task.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Submission is the final step, after classification, redaction, and review.

Options.text: Review the redacted document with a peer to confirm the redaction is complete.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Peer review of the redaction happens after redaction, which itself depends on classification first.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: Responsible data handling follows a strict sequence: classify sensitive content first, then redact it, then peer-review the redaction, and only then submit the sanitized document to Claude.

questions.topic: Purpose of an AI Governance Framework
questions.Question:
A knowledge worker is explaining the purpose of an organizational AI governance framework to a colleague.

Which description is most accurate?

Options.text: A governance framework defines approved tools, allowed data, required reviews, and reporting paths so AI is used consistently and accountably.
Options.reason: Correct. This captures the comprehensive scope of governance: sanctioned tools, data rules, review requirements, and escalation/reporting paths.

Options.text: A governance framework lists the AI tools the organization licenses and the cost of each, so users can pick the most cost-effective tool for each task.
Options.reason: Incorrect. A licensing/cost catalog is a procurement tool, not a governance framework.

Options.text: A governance framework defines the training every employee must complete before using AI tools, with separate requirements for each tool the organization licenses.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Training requirements alone cover only onboarding logistics, not the full scope of governance.

Options.text: A governance framework documents the AI policies the organization is legally required to adopt, focusing on regulatory compliance rather than day-to-day use.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Narrowing governance purely to legal mandates ignores its role in guiding daily operational use and quality.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: An AI governance framework is broader than any single concern -- it establishes approved tools, data rules, required reviews, and reporting paths together, ensuring consistent and accountable use across the organization.

questions.Question:
Your organization is building a customer support chatbot using Claude that needs to handle sensitive payment information. The chatbot will be integrated into your existing CRM system and must comply with PCI-DSS regulations.

Which of the following is the most appropriate governance approach for this use case?

Options.text: Pass all customer payment data directly to Claude for analysis, then implement post-processing filters to remove sensitive information before storing results.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Post-processing filters cannot guarantee removal of information already processed; this violates PCI-DSS data-minimization principles.

Options.text: Configure the system to exclude payment card data from Claude prompts entirely, use separate tokenization systems for payment processing, and document the data handling policy for audit purposes.
Options.reason: Correct. Never sending sensitive payment data to Claude eliminates the risk category entirely, and tokenization plus documentation supports both security and auditability.

Options.text: Use Claude's built-in encryption features to secure payment data before sending it to the API, then store the encrypted results in your CRM.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Claude does not provide application-level encryption that protects data once received; TLS in transit is not the same as application-level protection, creating false confidence.

Options.text: Implement a sampling approach where only 10% of payment transactions are sent to Claude for analysis to reduce exposure.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Sampling doesn't reduce compliance requirements -- any amount of unencrypted payment data sent to an external service violates PCI-DSS regardless of volume.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: The strongest PCI-DSS governance posture excludes payment card data from Claude entirely, using tokenization and clear documentation -- eliminating the risk category rather than trying to manage it downstream.

questions.topic: Preparing Feedback File with Mixed Content
questions.Question:
You are an operations team member preparing inputs to summarize customer feedback. The feedback file mixes public quotations with personal contact details.

Which preparation approach is most appropriate?

Options.text: Extract only the feedback content needed for the summary, redact or anonymize personal contact details, and submit the trimmed input.
Options.reason: Correct. This applies the principle of using the minimum necessary data -- keeping the useful feedback content while protecting personal details.

Options.text: Submit the entire file unchanged so Claude has complete context.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Submitting unredacted personal contact details unnecessarily exposes sensitive information.

Options.text: Replace the feedback content with the personal contact details and ask Claude to invent the missing feedback.
Options.reason: Incorrect. This backwards approach discards the actual useful content and invents fabricated feedback.

Options.text: Strip out the feedback content and submit only the personal contact details.
Options.reason: Incorrect. This removes exactly the content needed for the summarization task while retaining only the sensitive data.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: The right approach extracts only what's needed for the task (the feedback itself) while redacting or anonymizing personal contact details -- following the minimum-necessary-data principle.

questions.Question:
An HR associate is preparing to use Claude on a sensitive personnel matter. The organization's AI policy explicitly states that information related to ongoing investigations must not be entered into AI tools.

Which response best aligns with the policy?

Options.text: Enter the investigation-related information into Claude only after the investigation closes, since the policy applies during the investigation period.
Options.reason: Incorrect. This doesn't address what to do right now, during the active investigation, which is the actual situation at hand.

Options.text: Enter a paraphrased version of the investigation-related information that removes identifying details, since paraphrasing addresses the spirit of the policy.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Paraphrasing doesn't override an explicit organizational restriction on entering investigation-related information at all.

Options.text: Enter the investigation-related information into Claude in an Incognito chat, since Incognito chats do not retain information and therefore fall outside the policy's intent.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Using Incognito mode does not override an organization's explicit AI policy; data-handling restrictions apply regardless of chat mode.

Options.text: Refrain from entering investigation-related information into Claude and consult HR leadership for an approved alternative way to handle the matter.
Options.reason: Correct. The associate should follow the explicit policy now and seek an approved alternative workflow from HR leadership, rather than finding workarounds.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: When policy explicitly prohibits entering certain information into AI tools, the correct response is to follow that policy now -- refraining from entry and consulting leadership for an approved alternative -- not to paraphrase, delay, or use Incognito mode as a workaround.

questions.Question:
You are an HR specialist reviewing data items proposed for inclusion in a Claude prompt for a routine task.

Which two data items are appropriate to include? (Select 2)

Options.text: A redacted job description that the model will adapt for a posting.
Options.reason: Correct. A redacted job description provides needed role information without exposing unnecessary sensitive employee data.

Options.text: Accommodation request notes from an employee's HR file needed to draft a role-adjustment memo.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Accommodation notes contain highly sensitive personal information that shouldn't be entered for a routine task without specific policy authorization.

Options.text: Employee ID numbers and hire dates for the team roster included to help Claude personalize onboarding communications.
Options.reason: Incorrect. IDs and hire dates are unnecessary personal data for most onboarding-writing tasks; non-sensitive placeholders would suffice.

Options.text: A compensation-band summary that includes employee names and current salary figures for a specific team.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Names combined with salary figures are sensitive personnel/compensation data unnecessary for a routine prompt.

Options.text: An anonymized summary of an HR policy that the model will rephrase.
Options.reason: Correct. An anonymized policy summary provides the needed content for rewriting without exposing any identifiable employee information.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: Appropriate data items follow the minimum-necessary-data principle: a redacted job description and an anonymized policy summary both provide what's needed for the task without exposing sensitive personal or compensation information.

questions.Question:
You are a Claude associate assessing a proposed Claude use case before approving it for your team.

Which is the correct order of assessment steps?
(1) Compare the use case against the organization's policies and the relevant regulatory considerations.
(2) Document the assessment outcome and the rationale for traceability.
(3) Identify the audience, decision impact, and reversibility of the outputs.
(4) Decide whether the use case proceeds, requires modification, or is declined.
(5) Identify the data types involved and whether sensitive data is implicated.

Options.reason: Incorrect. Data-type identification (5) should come right after audience/impact (3), before comparing against policy (1).
Incorrect. Comparing against policy (1) too early, before audience/impact (3) and data types (5) are even understood, is premature.
Incorrect. Identifying data types (5) before establishing audience and impact (3) skips the step that determines the level of scrutiny needed.
Correct. Identify audience/impact/reversibility first, then the data types involved, then compare against policy/regulatory requirements, then decide, then document.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: A sound use-case assessment begins with audience/impact/reversibility (this determines scrutiny level), then identifies data sensitivity, then compares against policy and regulation, then decides, then documents for traceability. This ordering is independently corroborated by third-party CCAO-F reference sources.

questions.Question:
You are designing a system to help a financial services company analyze customer account inquiries and route them to the appropriate department. The company requires that all outputs include explicit reasoning before Claude reaches a conclusion. Currently, your initial tests show Claude sometimes routes inquiries to the wrong department without sufficient justification.

Which prompting technique would most directly address this issue?

Options.text: Implement chain-of-thought prompting that requires Claude to enumerate key details from the inquiry before making a routing decision.
Options.reason: Correct. Chain-of-thought prompting improves reasoning by requiring the model to work through intermediate steps (account type, issue category, customer segment) before deciding, increasing transparency and reducing errors.

Options.text: Switch to a smaller Claude model variant to reduce latency in the routing system.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Model size doesn't directly address reasoning quality or justification; smaller models typically produce less reliable reasoning.

Options.text: Increase the temperature parameter to encourage more diverse routing suggestions.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Increasing temperature increases randomness rather than improving systematic, justified analysis.

Options.text: Remove the system prompt entirely and rely only on the user message for context.
Options.reason: Incorrect. The system prompt is crucial for setting role, constraints, and output format expectations -- removing it would hurt, not help.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: Chain-of-thought prompting -- requiring Claude to enumerate key inquiry details before deciding -- directly increases transparency and reduces routing errors caused by incomplete reasoning.

questions.Question:
You are a project manager working through a long planning conversation with Claude and must keep the conversation productive as it grows.

Which two practices keep a long planning conversation productive? (Select 2)

Options.text: Open a new thread for every minor follow-up question to keep threads short.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Fracturing every minor question into a new thread breaks contextual continuity unnecessarily.

Options.text: Restate constraints and goals when the focus shifts to a new subtopic.
Options.reason: Correct. Explicitly restating key constraints and goals when the focus shifts anchors the model's attention on active parameters, preventing drift.

Options.text: Periodically summarize decisions made so far to compress the working state.
Options.reason: Correct. Context compression -- consolidating milestones and decisions into a dense summary -- reduces token overhead and prevents drift/hallucination.

Options.text: Switch context aggressively between unrelated planning topics within one thread.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Aggressive topic-switching within one thread pollutes attention and degrades coherence.

Options.text: Avoid summarizing so the model retains every original word it has produced.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Avoiding summarization accelerates context bloat and degrades performance rather than helping.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: Long conversations stay productive when you restate key constraints/goals at subtopic shifts and periodically summarize decisions to compress context -- fragmenting threads, aggressive topic-switching, and avoiding summarization all hurt coherence.

questions.topic: Using Feedback to Improve Work Over Time
questions.Question:
A knowledge worker is explaining how to use feedback to improve Claude-supported work over time.

Which description is most accurate?

Options.text: Capture general impressions after each run and apply them as broad prompt rewrites, since broad rewrites cover more potential issues than targeted changes.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Broad rewrites make it hard to determine what actually improved or degraded output; targeted changes are more reliable.

Options.text: Capture feedback as an aggregate quality score per run, since aggregate scores show whether quality is improving without requiring detail on individual issues.
Options.reason: Incorrect. An aggregate score alone doesn't reveal what specifically went wrong or needs to change.

Options.text: Capture specific feedback after each run, translate it into targeted prompt or workflow changes, and observe whether subsequent runs improve.
Options.reason: Correct. This creates a continuous, evidence-based feedback loop: specific feedback -> targeted change -> observed effect.

Options.text: Capture feedback only after several runs so patterns emerge from the volume of observations, then apply changes based on the patterns rather than any single run.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Waiting several runs before capturing feedback delays important improvements and lets the same problem persist.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: The most effective feedback loop captures specific issues after each run, translates them into targeted changes, and observes the effect on subsequent runs -- rather than waiting for patterns, using vague impressions, or relying on aggregate scores alone.

questions.Question:
You are a project lead reviewing a teammate's habit of using the same prompt template for every task regardless of type.

Which feedback is most warranted?

Options.text: The prompting strategy should be adapted to each task type because one template does not produce equally strong outputs across all tasks.
Options.reason: Correct. Different tasks need different instructions, context, constraints, examples, and formats -- a one-size-fits-all template can't serve them all equally well.

Options.text: The habit is ideal because a single template guarantees consistent quality across all task types.
Options.reason: Incorrect. A generic template doesn't guarantee quality; different tasks have different requirements a fixed template can't address.

Options.text: The prompting strategy should not change between tasks because adapting it wastes time and adds no value.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Adapting prompts often improves output quality and reduces revisions, adding real value despite some upfront effort.

Options.text: Task type has no effect on the appropriate prompting strategy.
Options.reason: Incorrect. Task type directly affects the instructions, context, and format a prompt should include.

questions.CorrectAnswerExplanation: Prompting strategy should adapt to task type, since a single generic template cannot produce equally strong results across fundamentally different kinds of work.
